title: Unit 1 – Good Manners
content:
Presenter: Hello! (1) Welcome to our programme "The Traveller's Guide".
Ko Thura: Thank you.
Presenter: Let's start our programme. So, Ko Thura, (2) the first question is from Daw Thin Thin. She wants to know what she should do when she first meets Thai people.
Ko Thura: Well, Daw Thin Thin, most of the time shaking hands will be fine. But, when someone gives you a "wai" (3) that is a small bow with the hands held together close to the body, you must do like this.
Presenter: (4) Very useful advice, Ko Thura. The second question comes from U Nyi Nyi. He asks if there is anything he should or shouldn't do in Japan.
Ko Thura: OK, U Nyi Nyi. The Japanese culture is slightly different from the Myanmar culture. In Japan, you should take off your shoes when entering a house. And remember to place them neatly together (5) facing the door you came in.
Presenter: Hello! Welcome to our programme "The Traveller's Guide".
Ko Thura: (6) Thank you.
Presenter: Let's start our programme. Our next caller is Ko Kyaw Moe. He wants to know if (7) there is any important thing he should not do in Russia.
Ko Thura: (8) Absolutely, Ko Kyaw Moe. The most important one to remember is not to shake hands in a doorway. Also don't leave empty bottles on the dinner table in Russia – that's bad luck.
Presenter: Thank you, Ko Thura. And we've got time for (9) one more question. This is from Nilar. She would like to know how she should behave when she meets the Korean people for the first time.
Ko Thura: Well, Ma Nilar. The most important thing to remember is that South Koreans like to bow a lot. It is a good way of showing respect to them. The deeper you bow, the happier they are.
Presenter: (10) Very interesting, Ko Thura. Thank you for your patience and joining us.
Ko Thura: My pleasure.

title: Unit 4 – Emotional Well-being
content:
Nilar: Hello, Thazin. You look tired. (1) What's wrong with you?
Thazin: You know, (2) I've got a lot of pressure from my parents.
Nilar: Oh, I see. You're feeling stressed out. (3) You ought to find some strategies to relax before it gets worse.
Thazin: I think you're right. (4) What should I do?
Nilar: (5) You should have some time for leisure activities.
Thazin: (6) That's true. I haven't thought about it.
Nilar: You'd better socialize more. What I mean is (7) you should make time to see friends two or three evenings a week. Hanging out with friends is a good way to relax.
Thazin: (8) I see your point, but my parents wouldn't allow me to go out with my friends often.
Nilar: I see. (9) Why don't you exercise regularly? Physical activity produces chemicals in the brain that make you feel happy.
Thazin: OK, (10) I will do that. Thank you for your suggestions.

title: Unit 5 – Colours
content:
Host: Colours influence everything from our appetite to our productivity. So, (1) here to tell us what the four most popular colours truly mean, we are delighted to welcome a colour psychologist Dr. Thiri.
Dr. Thiri: Good to see you. (2) Thanks for having me.
Host: Colours really do send a message without being overt, and also tell you about your own mood, productivity, etc. can be changed by colours. (3) So let's start with the colour red. What does it say if you wear red or if you have red in your home?
Dr. Thiri: So, red is the colour of passion. It can also represent aggression. It's a great colour for a female to wear because it draws attention. (4) Interestingly, red is also an appetite stimulant, so if you use a red plate while eating, it will make you want to eat more.
Host: Really? I see. This must be a reason why a lot of fast-food restaurants use red.
Dr. Thiri: (5) Absolutely yes. It stimulates your digestion.
Host: Should we change the story with blue?
Dr. Thiri: Yes, blue is the colour of (6) the sky and the ocean. Nearly 33 percent of businesses use blue as their primary brand colour. On top of that, blue conveys strength and dependability.
Host: Let's say if you painted your office wall (7) blue. It would help you have more work done.
Dr. Thiri: (8) Absolutely right. Blue makes you feel more productive.
Host: And, finally, purple.
Dr. Thiri: This is the perfect colour to pair with grey. Purple is the colour of luxury, royalty and wisdom. The colour can't necessarily dictate your behaviour but (9) it can help you.
Host: (10) That's fascinating. Thanks for your informative talk.

title: Unit 7 – Pollution: A Hazard to Our Environment
content:
Khant Hpone: Hi, Kaung Htet. You look so tired. What have you got in the bag?
Kaung Htet: Hello, Khant Hpone. They are my old UPS and (1) broken printer. I'm not going to use them anymore because I've got new ones.
Khant Hpone: You are going to throw them away, aren't you?
Kaung Htet: Right! I'll put them in the dumpster.
Khant Hpone: Oh, no. (2) Electronic waste like these is non-biodegradable. If they are brought to a landfill site, they won't break down and will remain on the land for at least 50 years. That's why, deadly chemicals from e-waste will (3) contaminate the soil and leak into water bodies.
Kaung Htet: Hmm. I might be responsible for land and water pollution.
Khant Hpone: Sure! Do you notice that we produce about 40 million tons of electronic waste every year worldwide but only 12.5% of them are recycled? So it means among the whole (4) toxic waste all over the world, e-waste comprises 70% of toxic waste.
Kaung Htet: Toxic waste! How can e-waste be harmful to our life?
Khant Hpone: These electronic things contain (5) deadly chemicals like mercury, lead and arsenic. As you've learnt in science lessons, (6) combustion of e-waste emits gases which can damage our central nervous system and kidneys. What a surprise! Even lower levels of lead can (7) damage a child's mental development.
Kaung Htet: Oh, I see. They're really harmful to us. But my apartment is quite small and I have no space to keep these old gadgets. What should I do?
Khant Hpone: If I were you, I would give them to other people who were in need. I usually post my e-waste on the website like 'Freecycle'. In this way, I can give my old one to a person in need. There is also an alternative.
Kaung Htet: Interesting. What's that?
Khant Hpone: You can send it to a certified e-waste recycler. Then it will be recycled in a safe and responsible way.
Kaung Htet: Wow! Great idea. That's a good way to prevent environmental (8) pollution. I'll use these ways instead of throwing my old things away. Thanks a lot. Bye!
Khant Hpone: Don't mention it. I'll contact you if I find those who are in need. Bye!

title: Unit 8 – Renewable Energy
content:
Student A: What is (1) your opinion on constructing a hydropower plant?
Student B: I think (2) it is expensive to construct and maintain a hydropower plant and this can have a negative effect on the local environment.
Student A: (3) I'm afraid I don't share that point of view. It doesn't produce air or water pollution, as opposed to burning fossil fuels like coal or gas.
Student B: (4) I am not sure about that. However, I'm sure building dams could damage the local ecological system and cause land behind the dams to flood.
Student A: (5) I have to side with you on that one. On the other hand, once a hydropower dam is up and running, the cost of maintenance and employee wages is relatively low although the initial installation cost is high.
Student B: That's true. Well, I think (6) we're going to agree to disagree. It is undeniable that there are certainly pros and cons of hydropower plants and it's an efficient means of producing electricity for a sustainable future.

title: Unit 9 – Helen Keller
content:
Host: Hello, everyone. (1) Welcome to our programme: The International Day of Disabled Persons Contest 2023. We have five brilliant high school students here with us to take the test. They are Nyi Nyi, Moe Moe, Nyein Chan and Shwe Yee.
Nyi Nyi, Moe Moe, Nyein Chan and Shwe Yee: Mingalarbar!
Host: (2) Today, I am going to ask you 20 questions related to the International Day of Disabled Persons and also famous people with disability. Is that clear to you?
Students: (3) OK. Here we go!
Host: (4) Very good! First question: Who is the famous deaf-blind author and activist?
Student: (5) I think it's Helen Keller.
Host: Correct. Helen Keller was the first deaf-blind graduate in the world. My third question is "Do you know the name of a famous music composer with hearing impairment?" Contestant 3 Moe Moe, please?
Moe Moe: (6) That's Ludwig Van Beethoven. His Piano Concerto No. 5 "Emperor" is my favourite. I heard it playing when I came into this room.
Host: Fantastic! Beethoven was a famous music composer.
Nyein Chan: Well, I have heard of Beethoven from my father, (7) who is a musician. It seems he continued to hear music in his mind's ear even though he was physically deaf.
Host: Perfect. (8) Actually, his loss of hearing could not stop him from composing beautiful music like these concertos. Now, I have a question for Shwe Yee. Do you know the name of a physically disabled scientist, who was famous for his discovery that black holes emit radiation?
Shwe Yee: (9) Dr Stephen Hawking.
Host: (10) Bingo! Well, his discovery has made the study of black holes a success.

title: Unit 11 – A Day's Wait
content:
Yoon Yati: Hi! Sandy, where are you going?
Sandy: Hi! Yoon. (1) I'm going to the library. I want to renew this book so that I can finish it at the weekend. If you're free, would you like to accompany me?
Yoon Yati: Actually, I borrowed a documentary film yesterday. Anyway, (2) I will come along with you.
Sandy: OK, let's go.
Yoon Yati: (3) What would you like to borrow?
Sandy: (4) As a matter of fact, I haven't decided yet. I'll browse the shelf, first. And what are you going to borrow? I mean – short stories, novellas or novels.
Yoon Yati: I (5) prefer short stories and novellas as they are not as thick as novels.
Sandy: I usually read books that are not difficult to understand.
Yoon Yati: By the way, what's the title of the book (6) that you're holding?
Sandy: It's Hemingway's "Nick Adams Stories".
Yoon Yati: Is he the same author (7) who wrote "A Day's Wait"?
Sandy: Yes, of course. He is a novelist, short-story writer and journalist.
Yoon Yati: I've heard of him.
Sandy: I've read (8) some of his works like "The Snows of Kilimanjaro".
Yoon Yati: I find "A Day's Wait" interesting. This reminds me of the first line of a poem by Alexander Pope – "A little learning is a dangerous thing".
Sandy: That's why we need to read more, learn more and explore more as long as we breathe in and breathe out.
Yoon Yati: Well, (9) I've got an idea. I would try reading his novella "The Old Man and the Sea".
Sandy: Great! It's about a story of an old man who suffered considerable hardship. Hemingway won the Pulitzer Prize for the fiction. I hope you'd like it.
Yoon Yati: (10) Which one will you borrow?
Sandy: For me, I will renew and finish reading this book, first. I have to do my take-home assignment tonight.
Yoon Yati: Oh, we haven't noticed. Let's take out our library cards.
Sandy: There's complete silence.
Yoon Yati: Yeah, I like this atmosphere.
Sandy: Me, too.

title: Unit 12 – Intercultural Communication
content:
Yadanar: It's nice to see you here again. Did you have a good time in Japan?
Nan Su: Oh, it's great! (1) I stayed there for a month.
Yadanar: Did you? Lucky you! Did you visit any famous places there?
Nan Su: (2) Yes, quite a number of famous places. I visited Hokkaido in February to enjoy the Sapporo Snow Festival.
Swan Htet: Really? That sounds amazing.
Yadanar: What kind of festival is it?
Nan Su: (3) It's a snow festival annually held in Sapporo. About two million people came to see hundreds of snow statues and ice sculptures in the Odori Park. The International Snow Sculpture Contest was also held in the park.
Yadanar: (4) Wow! Interesting! What did you see there?
Nan Su: Statues of famous buildings, well-known people, popular events and so on. Around 400 in total. There're a number of stages made of snow! Some musical performances were held on those stages.
Swan Htet: (5) What a great idea! What did you do there? Did you sing on the stage?
Nan Su: No way! But we enjoyed the long snow and ice slides. We also walked through a huge maze made of snow.
Swan Htet: That's amazing! I wish I were also there!
Yadanar: Me too! By the way, did you try any Japanese specialties?
Nan Su: Yes, I did. Hokkaido is famous for a variety of local foods – Sushi, Sashimi, Lamb BBQ, Hokkaido Ramen... and fresh fruits such as peaches, cherries.
